target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would remove work/school barriers for most voters
objection: A federal holiday does not automatically give private-sector workers paid time off, so many low-income retail and service workers would still have to work or lose pay; therefore the holiday would not, by itself, remove the main voting barrier for them.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday would increase turnout and democratic participation
objection: Research indicates that an election holiday by itself is not an effective way to raise turnout compared with other voting-access reforms, so the holiday is unlikely to produce large participation gains on its own.

target: AG1’s proposal that Election Day should be a national holiday instead of focusing on other reforms
objection: State-level measures such as employer time-off-for-voting requirements and automatic voter registration are more reliable ways to improve voting access than adding a holiday.

target: AG2’s claim that a federal holiday won’t remove work/school barriers because it does not guarantee paid leave
objection: The key issue is time availability, not whether time off is paid; if schools and many workplaces close or reduce hours on a holiday, voters gain usable time even without universal paid leave.

target: AG2’s claim that other reforms are a reason to reject a holiday
objection: Voting-access reforms like employer time-off rules and automatic voter registration can be pursued alongside a holiday, so their existence is not a reason to reject the holiday as ineffective or inappropriate.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday’s main effect would be limited because it doesn’t mandate paid leave
objection: A holiday can motivate civic participation by treating voting as a celebration rather than a chore, so it can increase democratic engagement through a separate motivational mechanism even if pay is not guaranteed.

target: AG2’s claim that broad public support and international practice do not matter
objection: The fact that 71% of Democrats and 59% of Republicans support the measure, and that many OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays, shows the policy is broadly supported and workable.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday by itself would not meaningfully improve voting access
objection: A designated civic holiday would let schools, election officials, and community organizations coordinate reminders, education, and registration help around Election Day, reducing information and friction barriers to voting.

target: AG2’s claim that low-income workers would still be blocked by work schedules
objection: If polling places have enough staffing and longer hours, voters can use the extra capacity; a holiday increases the pool of available poll workers, which can improve polling-place staffing and access even for shift workers.

target: AG2’s claim that lack of paid leave means low-income workers cannot vote on Election Day
objection: Voters are not limited to Election Day daytime voting because early voting and absentee/mail voting are available, so the absence of universal paid leave does not fully determine whether they can vote.

target: AG2’s claim that a federal holiday should be rejected because more reliable reforms exist
objection: A holiday can be adopted at the same time as other reforms like employer time-off rules and automatic voter registration, so the existence of better-targeted reforms does not justify rejecting the holiday altogether.

target: AG2’s claim that registration-focused reforms and time-off rules can replace a holiday
objection: Automatic voter registration and related reforms mainly reduce administrative friction, not the core problem that many people lack time to vote on Election Day; time-off laws also depend on employer compliance and enforcement, so they are not uniform nationwide solutions.

target: AG2’s claim that school scheduling does not matter enough to justify a holiday
objection: Parents and guardians often face weekday constraints tied to children’s school or daycare schedules, and making Election Day a holiday would reduce those caregiving and school-related barriers for them.

target: AG1’s assumption that a federal holiday would not interfere with other reform efforts
objection: Because policy bandwidth is limited, enacting a high-profile federal holiday can crowd out or delay more targeted state reforms such as employer time-off requirements and automatic voter registration.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would not reduce momentum for more targeted reforms
objection: Once a national holiday is enacted, politicians and advocates may treat it as a substitute for other changes, reducing urgency and political momentum for stronger state-level reforms.

target: AG1’s use of broad public support to argue that a holiday would complement other reforms
objection: Broad support for a holiday does not imply similar support for employer time-off mandates or automatic voter registration, so those more burdensome reforms may still lack the coalition needed to advance once the holiday is passed.

target: AG1’s claim that a federal holiday would not block or delay state reforms
objection: Even if a holiday does not legally prevent state action, it can reduce political urgency, make lawmakers think the problem is already solved, and thereby slow or stall later state reforms.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would reliably remove scheduling barriers
objection: A federal holiday does not reliably force employers, schools, or care providers to close or to give usable time for voting, so many work, school, and caregiving barriers would remain.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday helps low-income workers vote without paid leave
objection: A federal holiday does not guarantee paid time off, and many low-income hourly workers cannot absorb lost wages, so the policy does not solve the binding wage barrier to voting.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday’s civic-salience effects are enough to overcome worker barriers
objection: Even if a holiday increases motivation or civic salience, that alone cannot overcome the practical lost-wage barrier faced by many low-income workers.

target: AG1’s claim that a federal holiday would not inherently reduce incentives for additional reforms
objection: Employers can argue that employer time-off mandates are redundant once Election Day is already a federal holiday, and that argument can strengthen resistance to additional state reforms.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would produce meaningful voting-access benefits
objection: Because many low-income workers in retail and service jobs still would not get paid leave, a federal holiday is likely to yield only limited turnout improvements relative to more targeted reforms and may reduce incentives for those later reforms.
